summary: For ages 5–7, children describe and compare the external body structure of common animals across the five vertebrate groups (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals). The core objective is describe-AND-compare: moving from naming groups to describing external features (fur, feathers, scales, fins, wings, gills, legs, tail, beak) and comparing two animals from different groups side by side. The row treats body covering as the most reliable grouping cue for this age. A key point: group an animal by its body features, not by what it does (flying) or where it lives (in water).
misconceptions: Describing animals by colour, size or 'cuteness' rather than by structural features.
Assuming 'has scales' uniquely means fish — missing that reptiles also have (dry) scales.
Thinking all animals with four legs are the same group, or that 'has legs' distinguishes mammals.
Confusing wings as a bird-only feature — overlooking that bats (mammals) and insects also have wings.

activities.title: Side-by-side compare bench
steps: Place two animals from different groups next to each other — e.g. a robin beside a goldfish.
Name what each animal has (feathers, wings, beak vs scales, fins, gills) and identify shared parts (eyes, tail).
Tag each body part by placing/dragging a word label (wing, fin, fur, scale, gill) onto the correct part of each animal.
Swap one animal for a snake and notice that the reptile ALSO has scales — but dry ones, with no fins — so 'has scales' alone is not enough to tell the group.
Build up a five-group feature chart (covering, limbs, and — as a described feature only — how it moves) as more animals are compared.
activities.insight: Group-defining features emerge from directly comparing the whole set of features between two animals, not from any single clue. Body covering (feathers→bird, fur→mammal, scales→fish/reptile) is treated as the most reliable cue, but scales appear in more than one group, so you compare the full feature set. Movement is described, but grouping is decided by body structure, not by how an animal moves.

activities.title: Explore a labelled animal and its coverings
steps: Examine a fully labelled animal from each group, revealing part names (feathers, wings, beak; fins, scales, gills; fur, legs, tail) and the group each covering signals.
Say aloud 'birds have feathers', 'fish have gills and fins', 'mammals have fur' as each part is revealed.
Compare two labelled animals using a 'what's the same / what's different?' prompt between them.
activities.insight: Precise body-part vocabulary and the covering→group link are the tools used in every comparison.

activities.title: Handle real coverings and sort features to groups
steps: Handle real materials — feathers, fish scales, fur samples, close-up images of reptile skin — and match each to its group.
Sort feature cards under each group heading (feathers→bird, gills→fish, dry scales→reptile, fur→mammal, moist skin→amphibian).
Answer a short compare prompt: 'Name one body difference between a frog and a robin.'
activities.insight: Linking the tactile covering to the group makes external structure tangible and checks that the feature→group mapping is secure.

activities.title: Tricky cases: group by body, not by behaviour or habitat
steps: Consider: a bat flies and a robin flies, but only one is a bird — which one, and what body feature proves it?
Check the covering: the bat has fur and feeds its babies milk (mammal); the robin has feathers (bird). Group by feature, not by flight.

Decide whether a whale is a fish or a mammal by what you can check: whales breathe air through a blowhole and have no gills, have smooth skin rather than fish scales, have a few hairs (often only as babies) and feed their young milk, so they are mammals despite living in water.
Decide whether a penguin is a bird even though it can't fly: feathers make it a bird, not flight.
activities.insight: Animals are grouped by their body features (covering and parts), plus mammal traits like feeding young milk, not by what they do (flying) or where they live (in water). The bat is a mammal because it has fur and feeds its young milk; the whale is a mammal because it breathes air through a blowhole, has no gills or fish scales, and feeds its young milk; the penguin is a bird because it has feathers.

checkQuestion: A bat flies through the air and a robin flies through the air, but only one of them is a bird. Which one is the bird — and what could you look at on their bodies to be sure?
checkAnswer: The robin is the bird because it has feathers. The bat has fur, so it is a mammal. You tell the group from body covering (feathers, fur, scales), not from the fact that both can fly.
